newsitem.title: VATICAN: Glamorous ex-model swaps catwalk for convent.
newsitem.headline: Glamorous ex-model swaps catwalk for convent.

text.p: A glamorous Italian blonde, who scrapped a lucrative living as a catwalk model to work unpaid with the poor, returned to the limelight on Friday to tell the Vatican why she is thinking of becoming a nun.
Antonella Moccia, 30, was chosen as one of four people to explain their callings at a congress on religious vocations.
"The world of fashion fascinated her but she was looking for more and she found it among the poor," Nunzio Spinelli, the priest who first encouraged her vocation, told reporters.
"She found a greater love and satisfaction in God."
Moccia, a tall, willowy woman who showed for designers including Laura Biagiotti and Trussardi under the stage name Hella, was not expected to meet Pope John Paul at the ceremony.
But her testimony -- complete with video clips of her in action on the couture catwalks -- was set to take the Roman Catholic gathering by storm.
"I don't regret anything. Fashion has given me so much, but now I've found something more beautiful than fashion: service to Jesus Christ," La Repubblica newspaper quoted her as saying.

About 250 people from 37 European countries have been discussing how to make religious life attractive to young people, who live in an increasingly material society and are reluctant to espouse the Church's strict rules on celibacy.

The Vatican also faces the problem of an ageing priestly population. The number of priests fell by nearly 13 percent between 1978 and 1994, and the number of nuns by 24 percent, according to an official report released last October.
As well as Moccia, a former ballerina, an accountant who has joined a seminary and a deacon whose five sons are all priests will also explain their reasons for embracing the Church.
Spinelli, who handed out glossy photographs like a modelling agent, said Moccia wanted to avoid undue publicity. La Repubblica said she had been on a spiritual retreat.

But the priest told reporters how he met Moccia several years ago when he went to interview her for an article in a Roman Catholic magazine he edits about how, as a successful fashion model, she still had time for voluntary work.
He told how he had left her with the following thought: "If God wanted you all for himself, what would you do?
"She told me later that she had no peace of mind after that," Spinelli said. "Now she has found it in her vocation."
Moccia is the daughter of middle-class parents from Melfi, the southern town in Italy's poorest region where car giant Fiat has a modern factory.
Moccia began working with the nuns from Mother Teresa of Calcutta's Missionaries of Charity order in a Rome convent, helping out at a soup kitchen and caring for the homeless.
She subsequently gave up modelling altogether and Spinelli said she now wanted to join an order that helped young people.
Moccia has not yet taken vows but is preparing to live with a community of nuns to see if she is cut out for convent life. She has not said which order she plans to join.
